project.name: Not Arbitrary 03 — The Spade Is a Leaf

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Look at a club on a playing card. It is not a club, and it is not a clover. It is an acorn, drawn by somebody in a hurry.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, opening a story. The last sentence is the hook — land it plainly, no wink.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Five hundred years ago, German card makers took their suits from the forest and the hunt. This one is an acorn, hanging by its stalk.
entries.direction: Conversational, as if sketching while speaking.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: They called it Eichel. The German word for an acorn. Every card was a woodcut, cut and coloured by hand, and all that detail cost somebody an afternoon.
entries.direction: Reflective, with a small dry emphasis on the cost. Say the German word Eichel with a German colour, then say acorn plainly in English.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Then the French found a faster way. Print the outline once, and lay a stencil over it for the colour. But a stencil cannot cut a detail. It can only cut a hole.
entries.direction: Building, practical, three clear steps. A slight lift on the last sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: That is a club. Still an acorn, with everything expensive cut out of it.
entries.direction: Quiet satisfaction. Let the last phrase sit.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The next suit came off the same tree. A leaf, on its stalk. The Germans called that suit Laub, which simply means leaves.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: A stencil keeps the outline and throws away the inside. That is why a spade has a little foot at the bottom. It is a stem.
entries.direction: Matter of fact, then land the final sentence like a small discovery.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The third suit was a bell. A small round hawking bell, the kind tied to a hunting bird.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: But you never see a whole card. You see a corner of one, in a fan. A bell and a heart are both just round, so the bell had to grow corners.
entries.direction: Explaining a reason, warming into it. The last clause is the point.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Only one of the four never had to change. A heart was already a stencil. Two curves and a point.
entries.direction: Slower, a little warmth. The quiet middle of the film.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: So the pictures are German, and the printing is French. The names you use for them are neither.
entries.direction: A turn. Set it down cleanly and pause before the last sentence.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Italy and Spain never used the German suits at all. Their cards had swords on them, and heavy wooden sticks. England took the French pictures, and the Italian names.
entries.direction: Curious, building to the last clause.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: So you are holding a leaf and calling it a sword. An acorn, and calling it a stick. And a bell that grew corners so you could tell it apart from a heart.
entries.direction: Deliberate, one item at a time, like laying cards down.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: None of it was designed. It is a forest, cut down to fit a stencil, and misnamed for five hundred years. You have been holding the evidence all along.
entries.direction: Warm close, slowing into the final line.
